standard.title: Experiences and Perspectives — Colonisers, Settlers and First Nations Australians
standard.description: different experiences and perspectives of colonisers, settlers and First Nations Australians and the impact of these experiences on changes to Australian society's ideas, beliefs and values
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine perspectives of rulers and subject peoples and describe how contact shaped societies (AC9HH8K04, AC9HH8K09, AC9HH8K14). They have not yet examined the specific diversity of colonial Australian society — convict, free settler, and non-European experiences — or the contested language around colonisation and its ongoing significance.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the experiences of specific groups in colonial Australia — convicts, free settlers, non-Europeans, and First Nations Australians — examining how their experiences differed and how those experiences shaped changes to Australian society's ideas, beliefs and values, including the ongoing contestation of terms such as 'invasion', 'colonisation' and 'settlement'.

nodes.label: Convict experiences and their contribution to colonial society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the experience of convicts transported to Australia and examine how convicts contributed to colonial society — including how transportation offered social mobility unavailable in Britain.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the convict experience (transportation, assigned labour, emancipation) and give at least one example of a convict who made a significant contribution to colonial society.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the conditions of transportation and the convict system; explain how Australia's distance from Britain meant that the rigid British class system had less force — former convicts could accumulate land and wealth; examine specific examples (Francis Greenway, Samuel Terry) as evidence of social mobility; explain how convict origins shaped Australian cultural values (egalitarianism, anti-authoritarianism, mateship); examine the stigma and respectability debates among free settlers.
wider: Examine the experience from the perspective of free settlers who sought to distance colonial society from its convict origins — exploring the tension between convict contribution and free settler desire for respectability
Investigate the gendered experience of female convicts — how their experience differed from male convicts and how they have been historically represented

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat convict transportation as purely a punishment without understanding how it created social conditions — distance from Britain, labour needs, emancipation pathways — that enabled social mobility unavailable at home. Multiple examples across different types of convict experience build this picture.

success_criteria: Describes the convict experience including transportation, assigned labour and emancipation
Explains how transportation to Australia created conditions for social mobility different from Britain, with at least one example

nodes.label: Non-European experiences in colonial Australia
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the experiences of non-European groups in colonial Australia before 1900 — including Chinese miners, Japanese pearlers, South Sea Islanders, and Afghan cameleers — and explain how they contributed to and were treated by colonial society.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the experience of at least two non-European groups in colonial Australia, including their contribution and the discrimination they faced.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe Chinese miners on the Victorian and NSW goldfields — their scale of presence, contribution to the mining economy, the anti-Chinese violence and legal discrimination (restricted entry, special taxes); Japanese pearlers in northern Australia; South Sea Islander workers on Queensland sugar plantations (blackbirding and labour exploitation); Afghan cameleers in central Australia; explain how the treatment of non-European groups shaped the 'White Australia' policy that emerged at Federation; examine how these groups maintained cultural identity under discrimination.
wider: Examine the blackbirding of South Sea Islanders — the coercive recruitment of labour for Queensland sugar plantations — and evaluate where it sits on the spectrum from voluntary migration to forced labour
Investigate the legacy of a specific non-European community in Australia today — tracing the connection between colonial-era migration and contemporary Australian multiculturalism

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat colonial Australia as a binary settler-First Nations society without recognising the significant non-European presence. Multiple examples across different groups and regions build the more complex and accurate picture the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Describes the experiences of at least two non-European groups in colonial Australia, including their contributions and the discrimination they faced
Explains how the treatment of non-European groups connected to the development of White Australia ideology

nodes.label: First Nations perspectives and contested language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe First Nations Australian perspectives on and experiences of colonisation, and explain why terms such as 'invasion', 'colonisation' and 'settlement' continue to be contested in Australian society.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain why the same historical process is described differently ('invasion', 'colonisation', 'settlement'), identify whose perspectives each term reflects, and explain why the choice of term matters.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine First Nations perspectives on colonisation — what the arrival of Europeans meant, how it disrupted existing societies, cultures and connections to Country; explain the significance of language in historical accounts — 'settlement' implies peaceful occupation of empty land, 'invasion' implies hostile dispossession of existing inhabitants, 'colonisation' implies a structural process; examine why this contestation persists in public life today; connect to the terra nullius discussion from K03 as the legal underpinning of the 'settlement' framing.
wider: Examine specific instances where the language of 'invasion' vs 'settlement' has been publicly contested in Australia — parliamentary debates, school curriculum debates, ANZAC Day contexts — and analyse what is at stake in each instance
Investigate how First Nations communities describe their own historical experience using contemporary sources — connecting historical perspectives to present-day voices
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contested language question connects history to contemporary public debate in a way that is both intellectually substantive and civically important — it is one of the genuinely live historical debates students will encounter outside school. Examining specific instances of contestation builds skills in analysing how historical narratives function in public life.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat contested historical language as a matter of 'opinion' or 'sensitivity' rather than as a substantive question about whose perspective the account reflects. Making the link between language choice and perspective explicit — and showing that this has consequences for historical truth — is the key analytical move.

success_criteria: Explains why 'invasion', 'colonisation' and 'settlement' describe the same events differently
Identifies whose perspectives each term reflects and explains why the choice of term matters historically
